issues.what: The stem names the solution. Birds leave the foul-tasting kind alone, and the edible kind looks almost exactly like it, so 'birds shun them too' follows without knowing anything about mimicry. 'Birds sickened by the foul kind give up eating butterflies' is ruled out by 'the boldly patterned butterflies of one group', and the key is the only choice that uses the likeness to the foul kind at all.
issues.fix: Test the learning the mimicry rests on, by the rarity condition (F10). Keep the stem to '...looked almost exactly like them', add 'Bates found the look-alikes far scarcer than the foul kind.', then ask 'Suppose the look-alikes came to outnumber the foul kind many times over. What would most likely happen to them?' Key 'More would be eaten, as birds learn the pattern means a meal'; wrong 'Fewer would be eaten, with more of them to share the pattern', 'Just as few would be eaten, since birds never forget the pattern', 'More of the foul kind would be eaten in their place'.

issues.what: The question asks how the protein 'keep[s] the blood from freezing', so 'It lets the blood freeze solid and thaw unharmed' contradicts the question itself. Only three choices are live.
issues.fix: Replace it with 'It thickens the blood so ice cannot spread through it'.

issues.what: The ice-binding mechanism goes a step past the 8th-grade standard, which asks students to recognise polar-fish antifreeze as a physiological adaptation. It is told simply enough to stand at T4.
issues.fix: None needed. If the reviser prefers, the context can lead with 'a physiological adaptation, the body's own chemistry' before the mechanism.

issues.what: The key is an elementary fact: lizards bask in the sun to warm up and hide in shade or burrows to cool down, taught in grade 3-5 lessons on cold-blooded animals. The 1944 study is framing, and the key is also the only behavioural choice against three physiological ones. At T4 the question asks a 4th-grade fact.
issues.fix: Keep the study and ask about the cost the lizard's way saves (F20, F21): '...found that an active lizard kept its body near a temperature that suited it by moving between sun, shade and burrows. A desert mouse of the same weight keeps itself warm too. Why can the lizard live on far less food than the mouse?' Key 'It takes its warmth from the Sun, not from its food'; wrong 'It digests its food more fully than a mouse', 'Its scales hold in the heat its body makes', 'Its muscles waste less energy when it runs'.

issues.what: The stem gives 'venom that it injects through hollow fangs' as one adaptation. Fangs are structural, so 'Structural, structural, behavioural' can be defended by a careful reader, and the stem's own words invite that answer. The context has to argue that the venom, not the fangs, is the adaptation meant.
issues.fix: Name the venom alone: 'blotchy scales in the colours of the ground, venom that stuns or kills the rodents it bites, and a habit of lying still in ambush where rodents pass.'

issues.what: Independent origin (convergent evolution) is usually taught in high school. The reasoning it needs (gene changes that differ cannot have spread from one flow to the other) is within an 8th grader's reach, so it stands.
issues.fix: None needed. Optionally add to the stem 'Coat colour is inherited in these mice.' so that 'not inherited' is chosen only through a misreading of the gene evidence, not through doubt about the trait.

issues.what: The stem gives the answer away. 'The hares began to change on about the same dates every year, however early or late the snow came' rules out 'The first snow of the autumn' outright, and 'hares left white on bare brown ground' rules out 'The colour of the ground around it'. A change on fixed dates points to a calendar cue, and day length is the only one offered. The question keys a different fact from T2's lynx-hare cycle, as the lead asked, but it can be answered without knowing that fact.
issues.fix: Take the clue out of the stem and ask about the mismatch: 'Snowshoe hares turn white each autumn and brown each spring. Marketa Zimova, L. Scott Mills and their team followed nearly 200 radio-collared hares in Montana, where the snow now comes later and melts sooner than it used to. Many hares turned white on bare brown ground, and predators killed those hares more often. Why do the hares turn white before the snow comes?' Key 'Day length, not snow, sets off the change'; wrong 'The first frost sets it off, and frost comes early', 'Hunger sets it off, and food runs short early', 'Each hare learns the timing from its mother'.

issues.what: Lane: as written, the key is one species' moult trigger, a fact for the animal bank. The scope's general idea (an inherited trait that helps in one world can hurt in a changed one) sits only in the context.
issues.fix: The fix above ties the trigger to the mismatch, so the hare is evidence for the general idea; keep the context's last sentence on selection and the mismatch.

issues.what: The stem's own experiment rules out two wrong choices. Young birds raised in identical cages still 'tried to head the way [their] own parents had flown', so the route was not learned by following older birds, and it was not picked afresh for food each year. That leaves the key against 'Garden food changed the birds' genes for direction', the inheritance of acquired traits that T1 (webbed feet), T2 variation-and-survival (beetles) and T3 natural-and-artificial-selection (the sprayed flies) have already keyed against. The key itself, that the ones with the trait thrived and passed it on, is the selection fact keyed at T2 (beetles, ash) and T3 (antibiotics), and in this batch at genes ab23bb4c38 (carriers survive malaria).
issues.fix: Make Berthold's result the answer, so the T4 fact is that a behaviour's heading is inherited and differs between groups: 'Blackcaps, small songbirds that nest in central Europe, once flew southwest each autumn to winter around Spain. From about 1960 a few began flying northwest to Britain instead, where garden bird tables offer food in winter. Peter Berthold raised young birds of both groups in identical cages in Germany, where no older bird could show them a way. When autumn came, which way did each young bird try to fly?' Key 'The way its own parents had flown'; wrong 'Southwest, the old way of all blackcaps', 'Northwest, toward the richer winter food', 'No set way, with no older bird to follow'. The context then tells how selection spread the northwest heading over the generations.

unit_notes: Overlap check against every final.json and this batch. T1 adaptations-built-for-a-place keys camouflage, with mimicry only as a wrong choice; a646362384 goes deeper (how mimicry works), as it should. T1 born-knowing-or-learned keys instinct against learned; the blackcap fix keys something new (an inherited heading that differs between two groups). T3 natural-and-artificial-selection's peppered moths key matching the background; the pocket-mouse question keys separate origins, a different fact. T2 predators-partners-and-parasites keys the lynx-hare cycle; the hare question keys the moult trigger, a different fact, though see its tell. Balance: four of the nine questions rest on colouring (a646362384, ebb9e42cb8, 1a0c51da57, dd21427947). a646362384 and ebb9e42cb8 key nearly the same idea (predators that learned to fear the model spare the mimic), and the kingsnake context restates the Bates key in other words; the suggested Bates fix (the rarity condition) separates them. Behavioural adaptations carry only two questions (the lizards and the blackcaps), and both have high or medium issues; group hunting is unused (hibernation is rightly left out, since sources sort it both ways). Physiological is keyed twice by sorting (d5d45f2092, 74959e8c33) and once by mechanism (3bec34166d). Sweating and shivering, the scope's physiological temperature control, appear only as wrong choices; the suggested lizard fix brings the endotherm's cost into the key. Lanes: the species elsewhere serve as evidence for general ideas (mimicry, the three kinds, separate origins). Only the hare question's key is one animal's own fact, flagged there.
